title: Collectivisation and the Five-Year Plans
meta_desc: A-Level history adventure on collectivisation and Stalinist industrialisation.
final_note: You have seen socialism built at human cost.

walkthroughs.body_html: The 1927 procurement crisis convinced Stalin that NEP was politically unreliable. He defeated the Right Opposition (Bukharin, Rykov, Tomsky) by 1929. Forced grain collection from January 1928 (the Urals-Siberian method) presaged collectivisation. The 'great turn' of 1929 launched simultaneous collectivisation and industrialisation, dubbed by Stalin a revolution from above.

By March 1930, 58 per cent of peasant households were collectivised but resistance and Stalin's 'Dizzy with Success' article temporarily slowed the pace. Collectivisation resumed by 1931, reaching 93 per cent by 1937. Grain exports continued during the 1932-33 famine, which killed about 5-7 million in Ukraine, Kazakhstan and the North Caucasus, including the Holodomor.

walkthroughs.h2: Industrial outcomes of the Five-Year Plans
walkthroughs.body_html: First Plan (1928-32) targets were inflated yet pig iron rose from 3.3 to 6.2 million tonnes, electricity output trebled. The Second Plan (1933-37) developed Magnitogorsk and the Moscow Metro. The Third Plan (1938-41) prioritised armaments. Consumer goods stagnated; urban population grew from 26 million in 1926 to 56 million by 1939. Industrial expansion enabled Soviet WWII victory.

mcqs.q: How successful were Stalin's Five Year Plans?
options: The Five Year Plans were Lenin's last great achievement.
Heavy industry and steel output grew dramatically; consumer goods, quality and worker conditions lagged badly; statistics were inflated, but the USSR became an industrial power.
Collectivisation was suggested by Trotsky and Stalin opposed it.
The Five Year Plans turned the USSR into the most prosperous country in the world.

mcqs.q: Why did Stalin force collectivisation from 1929?
options: Collectivisation was suggested by Trotsky and Stalin opposed it.
To fund industrialisation by extracting grain, eliminate independent kulak farmers as a political threat, and impose Communist control on the countryside.
The Five Year Plans were Lenin's last great achievement.
Collectivisation was popular with peasants who wanted to share land.
Stalin took power because Lenin nominated him as his successor.
No — Lenin's Testament (1922-23) warned against Stalin's rudeness and recommended his removal; Stalin won by manoeuvring against Trotsky after Lenin's death.
Stalin took power by leading the Red Army to victory in the Civil War.
The Five Year Plans were Lenin's last great achievement.
